You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The testNormalDistributionImpl.testExtremeValues fails due to a ConvergenceException being thrown from NormalDistributionImpl.cumulativeProbability when called with very large or very small input values. The method cumulativeProbability uses the error function erf to compute the cumulative probability for a normal distribution. The erf function can throw a MaxIterationsExceededException if it fails to converge. 

The cumulativeProbability method catches this exception and checks if the input x is far in the tails of the distribution (using a threshold of mean ± 20 * standardDeviation). If so, it returns 0 or 1 respectively to represent the tail probabilities. Otherwise, it rethrows the exception.

When the test calls cumulativeProbability with extreme values such as Double.MAX_VALUE (very large) or similarly very negative values, the erf function may not converge, causing the MaxIterationsExceededException. The catch block in cumulativeProbability handles some extreme values by returning 0 or 1, but for some values between mean ± 20 * standardDeviation, the exception will be thrown again.

The test checks that for i > 9 (beyond 9 standard deviations), the lower tail should be less than 0.00001 and the upper tail greater than 0.99999, which roughly corresponds to tail probabilities near 0 and 1 respectively. The current implementation treats values beyond 20 standard deviations as tail-coded and returns 0 or 1, but values between 9 and 20 standard deviations do not get this special handling. This could cause non-convergence and exceptions for large but not quite extreme inputs, making the test fail with ConvergenceException.

Thus, the root cause is that the error function erf used in cumulativeProbability fails to converge and throw MaxIterationsExceededException for large input values near but less than 20 standard deviations away. The current fallback handling of these exceptions is incomplete, causing test failures when large inputs are used. The test suggests that the threshold for special tail handling should possibly be lowered from 20 to something smaller (like 9 or 10) or the error function implementation improved to handle larger inputs reliably.

Next, I will examine the source of Erf.erf and any related usage in this method or class to see why the convergence fails and if a fix is possible there or by changing the thresholds in cumulativeProbability.

messages.content:
The method Erf.erf(x) computes the error function as the regularizedGammaP with parameters a=0.5 and x^2, then negates if x < 0. The regularizedGammaP computes the lower incomplete gamma function via a series expansion if x < a+1, otherwise calls the regularizedGammaQ complement. 

In regularizedGammaP, the series expansion continues adding terms until the relative change is <= epsilon (1.0e-15) or maxIterations (10000) reached. If maxIterations is exceeded, it throws MaxIterationsExceededException. Also handles cases of infinite sums.

Based on this, the convergence exception is likely because for very large x, the series expansion does not converge fast enough within 10,000 iterations, resulting in the exception. The threshold in cumulativeProbability to trap tail values and short-circuit to 0 or 1 is set to 20 standard deviations. For values between 9 and 20, test expects tail probabilities close to 0/1 but the erf calculation sometimes fails to converge.

This shows the numerical implementation of erf via the regularizedGammaP series and maximum iteration limit causes failures for large inputs, especially those in the range near but less than 20 standard deviations from the mean. The cumulativeProbability method could trap a wider range with fallback tail values or improve the error function implementation to avoid convergence failures.

Next step: check regularizedGammaQ to see if it also can throw MaxIterationsExceededException or if it handles larger x more robustly. Also, check if cumulativeProbability or the distribution class has alternative fallbacks or supports larger iteration limits.

I will now check regularizedGammaQ method source.

messages.content:
The method regularizedGammaQ complements regularizedGammaP for cases where x >= a+1, using a continued fraction representation to improve convergence. This method also supports a maximum number of iterations and epsilon for convergence criteria.

It calls the method cf.evaluate(x, epsilon, maxIterations) on a specialized ContinuedFraction subclass to compute the value. Then applies an exponential/logarithmic factor and returns ret.

The continued fraction approach should have better numerical behavior than the series expansion when x is large, potentially improving convergence. However, it can also throw MaxIterationsExceededException if cf.evaluate fails to converge within maxIterations.

Thus, the MaxIterationsExceededException can occur both inside regularizedGammaP and regularizedGammaQ if the series or continued fraction approaches do not meet convergence criteria within maxIterations. This affects erf and indirectly cumulativeProbability.

Currently, cumulativeProbability sets a threshold at 20 standard deviations for tail coding to return 0 or 1 in case of failure, but the test expects proper behavior already for values beyond 9 standard deviations.

A fix can involve:
- Lowering the threshold in cumulativeProbability from 20 to 9 or 10 standard deviations to catch more tail cases and avoid exceptions;
- Increasing maxIterations or tweaking epsilon in regularizedGammaP/Q calls to improve convergence performance for larger x;
- Implementing better numeric approximations in erf for large arguments.

Currently, the exceptions are expected and caught in cumulativeProbability with fallback for extreme tails, but the threshold and numeric robustness are insufficient to pass the test for values between 9 and 20 standard deviations.

Next, I will review the test values (i = 0 to 100) and the exact ratio of i to standard deviations to confirm the expected range for tail coding and confirm the suggested threshold in comments.
The test loop uses a NormalDistributionImpl with mean=0, std=1. For i from 0 to 100:

- It asserts for i < 9 that lowerTail > 0 and upperTail < 1 (no tail coding yet).
- For i >= 9, asserts lowerTail < 0.00001 and upperTail > 0.99999 (tail probabilities close to 0/1).
- Comments say threshold was 9 because of tail precision issues; planned to raise to 30 after MATH-364 is fixed.
- cumulativeProbability current fallback is at ± 20 standard deviations.

This mismatch means cumulativeProbability throws exceptions when i between 9 and 20 because erf fails to converge, but test expects tail-coded results.

Summary: The bug occurs because cumulativeProbability catches MaxIterationsExceededException and only returns tail probabilities for inputs exceeding ± 20 standard deviations. For inputs in 9-20 std deviation range, it rethrows the exception causing test failures. The underlying convergence problem is due to the numerical error function implementation.

Possible fixes:
- Lower fallback threshold to 9 to align with test.
- Improve numerical stability of erf to avoid exceptions.

Hence, the failure is due to inconsistent thresholds and insufficient numeric convergence handling in NormalDistributionImpl.cumulativeProbability. The issue is that MaxIterationsExceededException from Erf.erf leads to an exception rather than returning tail-coded probabilities for moderate large inputs.

This explains the ConvergenceException reported in the bug report and test failure.
